content: 1. The mention of company names or products does not imply endorsement by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). 2. The Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 emphasizes the importance of protecting workers from the increasing number of occupational hazards. 3. NIOSH has implemented a program to evaluate the adverse health effects of chemical and physical agents, as well as industrial processes. 4. This document summarizes NIOSH's Occupational Hazard Assessment of Coal Liquefaction, which is part of that program. 5. Addressing hazards during the development of coal liquefaction technology can significantly reduce potential adverse health effects in experimental and commercial plants. 6. The full Occupational Hazard Assessment, Volume II, provides a detailed scientific and technical review of occupational safety and health issues in pilot plant operations. This summary document highlights key points in a more accessible format for a broader audience. 7. Both the full document and this summary are intended for use by workers, industry professionals, trade associations, government agencies, researchers, and the public. Those seeking a more detailed discussion should refer to the full Occupational Hazard Assessment of Coal Liquefaction. 8. The information and recommendations provided aim to assist in developing specific hazard control procedures for individual workplaces by those responsible for health and safety. 9. NIOSH will periodically update and evaluate new data and information as it becomes available and may propose standards to protect workers in commercial coal liquefaction facilities. 10. Coal liquefaction is a process that converts coal into hydrocarbon products, which involves the use and production of toxicants that may pose significant health risks to workers. 11. Toxicants in coal liquefaction range from simple chemicals to complex mixtures, including organic carcinogens, with varied potential health effects. 12. Animal studies have shown that some process chemicals can cause tumors at the site of application. 13. Workers may be exposed to these chemicals through inhalation of gases, vapors, or airborne particles, skin contact with contaminated materials, or accidental ingestion. 14. Some chemicals used in coal liquefaction have been linked to severe long-term effects, such as skin and lung cancer, in workers from similar industries. 15. Other potential adverse health effects include fatal poisoning from inhalation, severe respiratory irritation, and chemical burns. 16. Fires and explosions are also potential risks in coal liquefaction plants. 17. 18. Coal liquefaction is achieved by breaking the chemical and physical bonds of coal in the presence of a hydrogen source. 19. The four major coal liquefaction processes are pyrolysis, solvent extraction, direct hydrogenation, and indirect liquefaction. This assessment focuses on direct liquefaction processes. 20. In the United States, coal liquefaction technology is still in its developmental stages, with only a few process development units (PDUs) and pilot plants in operation. 21. Pilot plants primarily serve as testing grounds to determine optimal operating conditions for future commercial plants. 22. Projections suggest that by 1995, as many as 12 commercial-sized coal liquefaction plants could be operational, employing over 12,000 workers. 23. The total occupational safety and health impact of coal liquefaction technology must also consider the increased number of coal miners required. 24. 25. NIOSH's recommendations can be used to plan occupational safety and health programs and guide technology development. 26. The full-length document provides a thorough review of occupational hazards associated with direct coal liquefaction processes. 27. NIOSH has identified that chemicals and physical agents in coal liquefaction processes could pose serious health and safety hazards to workers unless precautions are taken. 28. One significant health hazard associated with coal liquefaction processes is cancer. 29. 30. Coal liquefaction materials applied to the skin of laboratory animals have produced cancerous growths. 31. Coal liquefaction materials have also caused adverse reproductive effects in laboratory animals. 32. Other chemicals found in coal liquefaction processes may adversely affect the respiratory and nervous systems, as well as the blood, liver, and kidneys. 33. Epidemiologic studies on coal liquefaction are limited, but there are strong implications from animal toxicologic and human epidemiologic studies on analogous compounds that certain agents in the coal liquefaction process pose serious health hazards. 34. 35. 36. 37. 38. Coal liquefaction processes operate above the autoignition temperature of many process materials, meaning leaks could result in immediate fires. 39. Many process materials are explosive, and leaks may create mixtures that exceed their lower explosive limit, potentially leading to explosions. 40. Specific health effects are described in detail, along with guidance on appropriate physical examinations and laboratory tests. 41. Skin effects are a major concern, as some chemicals in coal liquefaction processes can cause keratitis, skin cancer, and inflammation of hair follicles and sebaceous glands. 42. 43. Workers exposed to carbon black, refined petroleum solvents, coke oven emissions, and phenol may experience significant skin effects. 44. Skin sensitization may occur after contact with or inhalation of various chemicals. 45. Patch testing should only be used as a diagnostic aid after symptoms of skin sensitization appear and not as a screening technique, as it may cause sensitization. 46. Skin lesions should be monitored, with written and photographic records maintained. Changes in lesions should prompt referral to a dermatologist. 47. 48. Acute hepatotoxicity or severe cumulative chronic damage may occur before recognizable symptoms appear, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, weakness, malaise, and jaundice. 49. Screening tests for liver dysfunction include serum bilirubin, SGOT, SGPT, GGTP, and isocitric dehydrogenase. 50. 51. Inhalation of chemicals in coal liquefaction plants may damage the respiratory system. 52. 53. 54. Inhalation of coke oven emissions and coal tar products can cause chronic lung disease, including cancer. 55. Inhalation and pulmonary deposition of free silica can cause silicosis, a form of pulmonary fibrosis. 56. Chest X-rays and pulmonary function tests are recommended for screening respiratory health. 57. 58. Medical monitoring is essential to protect workers in coal liquefaction plants from adverse health effects. 59. 60. Comprehensive recordkeeping of employment history, medical history, and industrial hygiene data is critical for evaluating occupational hazards in coal liquefaction plants. 61. 62. Safety programs should include scheduled reviews, analysis of design, identification of potential hazards, and specification of safety controls and procedures. 63. Workers should be protected from flammable and toxic materials through adequate ventilation and proper disposal of gas purges. 64. 65. Instrumentation and controls should be provided to prevent plugging of lines and equipment through coking and solidification of coal slurries.
